items.excerpt: AI dominated keynotes, panels, and even opening remarks at the 35th International Publishers Association Congress in Kuala Lumpur (July 5-9, ~500 participants from 40 countries). Keynote speaker Thad McIlroy said publishing has moved past the 'golly-gee-whiz phase of AI' to the 'what the heck am I going to do about it?' phase, while IPA president Gvantsa Jobava called publishers' collective work 'the best source of training data for AI.'

Day-one coverage of the 35th IPA Congress in Kuala Lumpur, where the opening panel 'Ethics of Publishing: Accountability in the Age of AI and Misinformation' framed publishers as actively battling AI's ability to propagate misinformation at exponential rates and erode trust, alongside copyright and freedom-to-publish agendas.

Jamir Nazir won the 2026 Commonwealth Short Story Prize for 'The Serpent in the Grove' after an unprecedented review cleared him of AI-use allegations that had surrounded his regional-winner entry — a landmark case of a literary prize formally adjudicating AI suspicion against a writer.

Publishers are still waiting for 'clear' legal answers on AI training, outputs, and licensing, the Publishers' Licensing Services Conference heard — years of copyright litigation have yet to resolve the key questions publishers need answered before committing to AI licensing strategies.

Friedman highlights new research analyzing 500,000 anonymized ChatGPT conversations that identifies 'infinite story demanders' — a small cohort of power users generating large volumes of repetitive AI fanfiction and erotica for personal consumption — evidence that LLMs enable interactive, playful, permutating story consumption outside traditional publishing.

Cambridge University Press, COUNTER, and NISO convened nearly three dozen experts — libraries, AI tool developers, funders, publishers, platforms — to build frameworks that make AI use of scholarly content traceable and measurable: usage metrics, provenance, and attribution standards for generative AI systems.

Bryan Charles traces AI's slow, steady invasion of literary translation through the test case of translating Proust with ChatGPT, talking with translators Andrew Rothwell and Sam Taylor about how AI tools have reduced the 'cognitive load' of literary translation — and what is lost when they do.
